name: Mary I of England
role: Queen of England and Ireland (1553–1558), the first queen regnant crowned in England; wife of Philip II of Spain

born.place: Greenwich Palace (Palace of Placentia), Greenwich, England

died.cause: Illness; the exact cause is uncertain (an influenza epidemic and uterine or ovarian cancer have both been suggested)

summary: Daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon who, after being declared illegitimate and pressed to renounce her faith under her father and brother, became queen in 1553, reunited the English church with Rome, and revived the heresy laws under which about 280 Protestants were burned, earning her the later name "Bloody Mary."

key_dates.label: Declared illegitimate after her parents' marriage is annulled; stripped of the title of princess
Signs a submission accepting her father as Supreme Head of the Church and her parents' marriage as unlawful
Defies Edward VI's council by continuing to hear Mass; her household officers are imprisoned
Overthrows Lady Jane Grey's nine-day reign and becomes queen; Parliament repeals Edward VI's religious laws
Wyatt's rebellion suppressed; marries Philip of Spain; England reconciled to Rome by Cardinal Pole (30 November)
Heresy laws revived; burnings of Protestants begin with John Rogers (4 February)
Thomas Cranmer burned at Oxford; Reginald Pole becomes Archbishop of Canterbury
Calais, England's last possession in France, falls to the French (January)

accomplishments.text: Won the throne in July 1553 against the attempt by John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland, to crown the Protestant Lady Jane Grey, and became the first woman crowned queen regnant of England.

Under Mary the swing went back to Rome: Edward VI's English Prayer Book was abolished, the Latin Mass, altars, and images returned, married priests were removed from their parishes, and papal authority was restored, until her half-sister Elizabeth I reversed it again in 1559.
Restored Catholic worship. Parliament repealed Edward VI's religious laws in 1553, the Latin Mass returned, and married clergy were removed from their posts.

Reunited the Church of England with Rome. On 30 November 1554 the papal legate Cardinal Reginald Pole absolved the kingdom, and the Second Act of Repeal (1555) undid Henry VIII's anti-papal laws, though former monastic lands were left with their new owners.

Revived the medieval heresy laws (1555). Between February 1555 and November 1558 about 280 Protestants were burned, among them Archbishop Thomas Cranmer and Bishops Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, and John Hooper, and many ordinary men and women; others died in prison and some 800 fled abroad.

Supported a program of Catholic renewal under Pole: new preaching and catechetical books such as Bishop Edmund Bonner's homilies, a legatine synod (1555–1556) with plans for diocesan seminaries, and the refounding of some religious houses such as Westminster Abbey.

Married Philip of Spain (later Philip II) in 1554, a match that provoked Sir Thomas Wyatt's rebellion. After the rising was crushed, Lady Jane Grey, her husband, and her father were executed, along with about 90 rebels.

Took England into Spain's war with France (1557), which led to the loss of Calais in January 1558. Her two apparent pregnancies (1554–1555 and 1557–1558) produced no child, and the crown passed to her Protestant half-sister Elizabeth.

Became known as "Bloody Mary" through the Protestant memory of the burnings, shaped above all by John Foxe's Acts and Monuments (1563). Recent historians such as Eamon Duffy and Linda Porter have reassessed her reign, while acknowledging that the burnings were exceptional in English history.

sayings_intro: Few words are firmly attributed to Mary. This is a selection.

original.phrase: "When I am dead and opened, you shall find Calais lying in my heart"
original.reference: Reported in Raphael Holinshed's Chronicles (1577), as words spoken near her death
original.note: Not in her own writings; recorded about two decades later and possibly embellished. Usually quoted as "...you shall find 'Calais' lying upon my heart."

misattributed.note: Not her words. The name comes from later Protestant tradition built on Foxe's account of the burnings; it is also used for an unrelated cocktail and folklore figure.

misattributed.reference: English nursery rhyme, first printed in the 18th century
misattributed.note: Often said to be about Mary I and her executions, but there is no evidence connecting the rhyme to her; the link is a later theory.

victims_title: Notable people executed on Mary I's authority
victims_intro: About 280 people (Eamon Duffy counts 284) were burned for heresy in Mary's reign, the great majority ordinary laypeople in London, Kent, Essex, and East Anglia; others died in prison. In addition, Lady Jane Grey and about 90 rebels were executed after Wyatt's rebellion in 1554. Heresy cases were tried by bishops and papal commissioners and the burnings carried out by the secular authorities under the revived heresy laws, with the queen's warrant. Historians agree that Mary supported the burnings and refused to stop them; how far she, Cardinal Pole, Bishop Stephen Gardiner, Bishop Edmund Bonner, and the council each drove them is debated. This is a selection of the best-known cases. The links are Wikipedia searches for each name, and the Foxe link opens the online edition.

victims.name: Lady Jane Grey
victims.executed: Beheaded on Tower Green, Tower of London, 12 February 1554
victims.condemned_by: Tried for high treason at the Guildhall, London, November 1553
victims.allegation: The Protestant great-niece of Henry VIII, proclaimed queen for nine days in July 1553. Mary at first spared her, but signed her death warrant after Jane's father joined Wyatt's rebellion. A Catholic priest, John Feckenham, was sent to convert her before her death; she refused.
victims.verification_note: The queen signed the warrant; her earlier reluctance is also recorded.

victims.name: John Rogers
victims.condemned_by: Commission headed by Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester and Lord Chancellor, January 1555
victims.allegation: Editor of the Matthew Bible (1537) and a London preacher, he was the first Protestant burned under Mary.
victims.verification_note: Burned under the heresy laws revived in her reign and with royal authority. Her personal part in this case is not recorded.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

victims.name: John Hooper
victims.condemned_by: Commission headed by Stephen Gardiner, January 1555
victims.allegation: Former Bishop of Gloucester and Worcester and a strong Protestant reformer. He was sent back to his own cathedral city to be burned; Foxe describes a slow death in a fire of green wood.
victims.verification_note: Executed under royal authority in her reign. The details of his suffering come from Foxe.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

victims.name: Rowland Taylor
victims.executed: Burned on Aldham Common, near Hadleigh, Suffolk, 9 February 1555
victims.condemned_by: Commission headed by Stephen Gardiner, January 1555
victims.allegation: Rector of Hadleigh, arrested after he resisted the restoration of the Mass in his parish church.
victims.verification_note: Executed under royal authority in her reign; her personal part in this case is not recorded.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

victims.name: Hugh Latimer
victims.executed: Burned outside Balliol College, Oxford, 16 October 1555
victims.condemned_by: Papal commissioners led by John White, Bishop of Lincoln, acting under Cardinal Pole's legatine authority, October 1555
victims.allegation: Former Bishop of Worcester and Henry VIII's best-known Protestant preacher. Foxe records his words to Ridley at the stake: "Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man."
victims.verification_note: Executed under royal authority in her reign. The famous words are reported by Foxe, not in an earlier source.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

victims.name: Nicholas Ridley
victims.executed: Burned outside Balliol College, Oxford, 16 October 1555, with Latimer
victims.condemned_by: Papal commissioners led by John White, Bishop of Lincoln, October 1555
victims.allegation: Former Bishop of London, who had preached in 1553 that Mary and Elizabeth were illegitimate in support of Lady Jane Grey. Foxe describes his death as long and painful.
victims.verification_note: Executed under royal authority in her reign; her personal part in this case is not recorded.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

victims.name: Thomas Cranmer
victims.executed: Burned outside Balliol College, Oxford, 21 March 1556
victims.condemned_by: James Brooks, Bishop of Gloucester, as papal commissioner (September 1555); sentenced by Pope Paul IV (December 1555)
victims.allegation: The former Archbishop of Canterbury, who had annulled her parents' marriage in 1533. He signed several recantations, which under church law could have saved him, but Mary refused to pardon him. At the stake he withdrew his recantations.
victims.verification_note: Mary's refusal to spare him after his recantations is documented.

links.label: Foxe's Acts and Monuments online (search the name)

persecution_note: Before she became queen, Mary was declared illegitimate, separated from her mother, and pressed under threat of treason charges to accept her father's supremacy over the church, which she did in 1536. Under her Protestant brother Edward VI she was pressured to give up the Mass, and her household officers were jailed. Edward's will tried to exclude her from the throne. She was never imprisoned or excommunicated.

persecution.title: Declared illegitimate and separated from her mother
persecution.summary: After Cranmer declared Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon void (1533), Mary lost the title of princess and was declared illegitimate by the Act of Succession (1534). Her household was broken up, she was made to serve in the household of the infant Elizabeth, and she was not allowed to see her mother, who died in 1536.

responsible.name: Thomas Cranmer
responsible.role: Archbishop of Canterbury; declared her parents' marriage void

responsible.name: Anne Boleyn
responsible.role: Queen; reported by contemporaries to have encouraged harsh treatment of Mary

persecution.outcome: Kept from her mother and from court until 1536.

persecution.title: Forced submission to her father's supremacy
persecution.summary: After Anne Boleyn's fall, Mary still refused to accept Henry as head of the church or her own illegitimacy. A council delegation led by the Duke of Norfolk threatened her, judges advised that she could be proceeded against for treason, and her supporters were questioned. Advised by the imperial ambassador Eustace Chapuys to give way, she signed the submission.

responsible.name: Thomas Cromwell
responsible.role: The king's chief minister; managed the pressure and drafted the terms

responsible.name: Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk
responsible.role: Led the council delegation that confronted her

persecution.outcome: She signed, was restored to her father's favor, and returned to court, though still illegitimate in law until 1544, when Parliament restored her to the succession.

persecution.title: Pressure to abandon the Mass under Edward VI
persecution.summary: After the Act of Uniformity (1549) made the Book of Common Prayer compulsory, Mary continued to have Mass said in her household. In 1550 she considered fleeing to the Continent. In March 1551 Edward VI and his council confronted her; in August 1551 her chief officers, Robert Rochester, Edward Waldegrave, and Francis Englefield, were sent to the Tower for refusing to stop the Masses in her house.

responsible.name: Privy Council of Edward VI
responsible.role: Led by John Dudley, Earl of Warwick (later Duke of Northumberland)

defended_by.name: Emperor Charles V
defended_by.role: Her cousin; threatened war if she was denied her Mass

persecution.outcome: She continued to hear Mass privately, protected by fear of the emperor's reaction.

persecution.title: Excluded from the throne by Edward VI's "Devise"
persecution.summary: Edward VI, with the Duke of Northumberland, set aside both his half-sisters in favor of Lady Jane Grey, in large part to keep a Catholic from the throne. After Edward's death on 6 July, Jane was proclaimed queen and forces were sent to capture Mary.

responsible.name: Edward VI
responsible.role: Drew up the "Devise for the Succession"

responsible.name: John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland
responsible.role: Lord President of the Council; promoted the scheme and led forces against her

persecution.outcome: Mary gathered support in East Anglia, the council changed sides, and she was proclaimed queen on 19 July 1553. Northumberland was executed for treason.

excommunication_note: Mary was never excommunicated. She shared in the schism of her father's church after her forced submission of 1536, but the realm, including her, was formally absolved and reconciled to Rome by Cardinal Pole on 30 November 1554. She died in communion with the Roman Catholic Church.
persecuted_others_note: Mary I restored the old heresy laws and supported the burning of about 280 Protestants between 1555 and 1558, the 'Marian persecution' that gave her the name 'Bloody Mary' in later Protestant memory. She also had Lady Jane Grey and about 90 rebels executed after Wyatt's rebellion, and removed married and Protestant clergy from their posts; some 800 Protestants went into exile abroad.

persecuted_others.title: The Marian burnings (summary)
persecuted_others.targets: About 280 Protestants (Eamon Duffy counts 284), mostly laypeople, including John Rogers, John Hooper, Rowland Taylor, Hugh Latimer, Nicholas Ridley, and Thomas Cranmer
persecuted_others.summary: See the list of executed people above. Parliament revived the medieval heresy laws at the end of 1554 and the burnings began in February 1555; bishops and papal commissioners tried the cases and the secular authorities carried out the sentences. Mary supported the policy and refused to halt it; how far she, Cardinal Reginald Pole, Bishop Stephen Gardiner, and Bishop Edmund Bonner each drove it is debated by historians.

persecuted_others.title: Executions after Wyatt's rebellion
persecuted_others.targets: Lady Jane Grey, her husband Guildford Dudley, her father the Duke of Suffolk, Sir Thomas Wyatt, and about 90 rebels
persecuted_others.summary: After the largely Protestant rising led by Sir Thomas Wyatt against her Spanish marriage failed in February 1554, Mary signed the death warrant of Lady Jane Grey, whom she had earlier spared, and about 90 rebels were hanged. Her half-sister Elizabeth was sent to the Tower on suspicion of involvement but was not charged.

persecuted_others.title: Removal of married and Protestant clergy
persecuted_others.targets: Married priests and Protestant bishops and clergy
persecuted_others.summary: Royal injunctions of March 1554 ordered bishops to deprive clergy who had married under Edward VI; many were removed from their parishes, some later restored after separating from their wives. Protestant bishops such as Hooper, Ridley, Latimer, and Cranmer had already been deprived and imprisoned.
